21.text: Hotpot on the first cold night of the year. Nobody announces it, someone just fills the pot and everyone drifts toward the table.
We still write birthday letters instead of buying cards. My grandfather started it. I keep nineteen of them in a shoebox under the bed.
Loser of family game night does the dishes for a week. I have done so many dishes, and I would still riot if we ever stopped.
Sweeping the graves in April, then eating cold noodles in the cemetery parking lot like it's a picnic. Sounds grim. It's the opposite.
Everyone squeezes onto the one couch for the first snow of the year, even now that none of us remotely fit on it.
Dumplings on New Year's Eve, and my aunt hides a peanut in one. Whoever bites it gets a year of luck and a nearly chipped tooth.
The Sunday call to my grandmother, all of us passing the phone around the kitchen like a relay baton until the food gets cold.
My dad reads the same poem every Thanksgiving. Badly. On purpose, I suspect, so that all of us get to groan in unison.
We toast the empty chair first at every wedding and holiday. It keeps the dead at the table, which is where they belong.
Pancakes shaped like whatever animal you request. My mother's rabbits always came out looking like bears, and that was half the point.
Calling home before every flight, no matter the hour. My mother did it to her mother across an ocean. Now I do it to her.
One night every summer we all sleep on the porch. Bad backs, mosquitoes, whispered arguments about blankets. Never miss it.
Lighting a candle on the first morning of school, kindergarten through grad school. My grandmother swears it works. The report cards agree.
New pajamas on Christmas Eve. It is a small, slightly silly thing and I will defend it with my last breath.
After every funeral we cook the person's favorite dish and tell only the embarrassing stories. I hope my dish turns out worthy.
Measuring the kids on the kitchen doorframe every January first. Three houses now, and my father unscrews the doorframe and brings it along.

23.text: 'Lean on Me,' because somebody in this house is always carrying somebody else's groceries, rent, or heartbreak.
An old Taiwanese ballad my grandmother hums while washing dishes. Now all of us hum it without ever noticing we learned it.
Honestly, the lo-fi playlist I study to. All of us in one room doing completely different things, and somehow it holds together.
'La Bamba,' because every party ends with the uncles pushing the furniture back whether anyone asked them to or not.
Anything with a call and response. One of us starts, the rest can't help finishing. Dinner here is basically a choir with chopsticks.
'Somewhere Over the Rainbow,' the ukulele version. Gentle, a little off-script, and always playing at our beach bonfires.
A mariachi trumpet line. Loud, proud, slightly too much for the occasion, and it still makes everyone cry at weddings.
'Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da.' Life goes on in this family, always with a chorus that refuses to stay sad for more than a verse.
The rice cooker's little tune. I know it isn't music, but every single one of us starts drifting toward the kitchen when it plays.
'Stand by Me.' My parents danced to it in a church basement in 1987 and we have all been standing by each other since.
Something in a minor key that turns joyful anyway. Klezmer, basically. We cry, then we dance, occasionally in that order.
'Country Roads.' Not one of us is from West Virginia. All of us scream it in the car like we grew up there.
The real song is my father whistling while fixing something he should not be fixing. Off-key, confident, completely unstoppable.
'De Colores.' My grandmother sang it while shelling beans, and now that tune means everything is going to be fine.
A slow Cantonese ballad from the radio my grandfather kept in the shop. Static and all. Honestly, the static might be the family part.
'Here Comes the Sun.' Not because things are easy, but because we are all annoyingly certain the hard part is almost over.

25.text: My mother walking into an English class at fifty-three, taking the front row seat, raising her hand first.
My brother telling our parents he was leaving pre-med to teach middle school. The silence lasted a week. The pride lasted forever.
My grandfather left everything twice, one war and one border. He calls it luck. Nobody who saw his hands shake calls it luck.
My little sister returning a wallet with two hundred dollars in it during the year we had about thirty in checking.
My aunt asking for a divorce in a family where nobody had ever said the word out loud. She freed more of us than she knows.
Dad going back into the smoking garage for the dog. We yelled at him for a month and loved him double for it.
My cousin coming out at the new year dinner, right between the fish and the oranges. Grandma just added rice to his bowl.
My mother negotiating with the landlord in a language she had spoken for eight months. And winning. And getting the leak fixed.
Watching my grandmother bury her husband in the morning and then teach her piano students that same afternoon, door open, tea poured.
My son telling his coach he wouldn't play unless the benched kid got minutes too. He was nine. He sat out two whole games.
My father apologizing to me, fully, with no 'but' at the end. In our family that took more courage than any of the war stories.
My sister boarding a plane with two suitcases and a nursing degree nobody here would recognize, starting over at forty.
My uncle standing up at the funeral and telling the truth about his drinking with the entire family watching. Six years sober now.
My mom asking her boss for the raise she had rehearsed at our kitchen table for two straight weeks. She got it. We got pizza.
My grandmother hid a neighbor family's papers in her flour tin during the occupation. She told us about it like it was a recipe.
My daughter walking back into the school where the bullying happened, chin level, braids done. Bravery can be twelve years old.

27.text: Dumplings. Not because they're the best food, but because they're the only dish that requires eleven people and three arguments.
Tamales. Full assembly line, radio on, somebody burning their fingers on the husks, somebody quality-controlling the masa like it's customs.
My grandmother's chicken soup, with nobody allowed to write anything down. You learn it by being yelled at lovingly.
Homemade pasta. Flour on every surface, the dog underfoot, and one person insisting the sauce needs another hour. It does.
Hotpot, so that nobody actually has to cook and everyone gets to argue about whether the broth is spicy enough. It never is.
Paella in the biggest pan we own, outside, with the uncles supervising a fire that does not need six supervisors.
Bread. Something that makes us stand around together with nothing to do but talk while the dough takes its time rising.
Injera and three stews, everyone tearing from the same platter. Eating off one plate makes it impossible to sulk alone.
Pierogi, because pinching a hundred little dumplings shut is the cheapest group therapy currently available anywhere.
Honestly? Instant noodles, upgraded. Everyone brings one topping. We rate them. Last place does dishes. It's a tradition in progress.
Mooncakes from scratch, exactly once, so we finally respect the bakery in Chinatown that has been doing it right all along.
The full Sunday gravy. Sauce going by ten in the morning, meatballs vanishing off the tray before dinner. It's a heist and a meal.
Kimchi day. Gloves on, floor covered in newspaper, grandmother tasting the cabbage and judging our futures by the brine.
A birthday cake with no birthday attached. Lopsided, over-frosted, decorated by the youngest with total impunity.
My father's biryani, which takes five hours and requires all of us mostly to keep him company and guard the fried onions.
Whatever the oldest recipe card in the tin says. Half the measurements just say 'some.' That's the whole point of doing it together.

29.text: We all salt the pasta water like the ocean because Grandma did, and every one of our doctors has opinions about it.
Nobody in this family can leave a house without saying goodbye three separate times. My mother's doing. Departures run forty minutes.
We check the stove twice before leaving. All of us, every time. My father's worry, lovingly inherited, occasionally useful.
Saving every glass jar because 'it's a good jar.' My grandmother survived a war. We survived nothing and own four hundred jars.
We all read the last page of a book first. My aunt started it. We are monsters and we are at peace with that.
Answering 'how are you' with 'have you eaten.' Straight from my grandmother, and honestly it's the better question.
Talking to the GPS like it's a difficult coworker. Thanks, Dad. All four of us do it now, including the six-year-old.
We hum while we cook without noticing. I caught my brother doing it over midnight ramen and heard our mother exactly.
Arriving forty minutes early to every airport, appointment, and movie. My father's fear of lateness became the family religion.
Nobody throws away a rubber band. There is a drawer. There has always been a drawer. Grandpa's drawer now lives on in three states.
We apologize to furniture we bump into. My mother did it once, and now this entire family has impeccable manners toward chairs.
Pointing with our lips instead of our hands. My grandmother's move. My kids do it at school and confuse absolutely everyone.
The worse the news, the calmer my mother's voice got. We all do it now. You can measure a crisis here by how quiet the phone call is.
For worse: interrupting. For better: no silence in this family has ever once been awkward. Same uncle, both habits.
We all crack the window at night, even in January. My father's rule about fresh air outlived him, so now we are all a little cold, together.
Thank-you notes for everything, even terrible gifts. Especially terrible gifts. My grandmother's revenge, disguised as grace.

31.text: Dim sum in the Richmond at ten, carts and all. Golden Gate Park until the fog burns off. Ocean Beach when it doesn't. Home by dark for soup.
Bakery run in the Mission first, pan dulce while it's still warm, then Dolores Park with a blanket and absolutely nobody checking the time.
Sleep till eleven, meet everyone at the Ferry Building, sample things we won't buy, argue about which taqueria, end up at the usual one.
Fog until noon, so nobody rushes. Congee at home, then the long flat walk along the Great Highway with the grandparents setting the pace.
Early swim at Aquatic Park for the one brave cousin, coffee in North Beach for the rest of us, then watching the bocce old-timers and pretending we understand the rules.
Muni out to the Sunset, pastries on Irving, then the whole family flying one dollar-store kite badly at Ocean Beach for hours.
Alemany farmers market with grandma commanding the cart, then everybody cooking whatever she bargained for while the fog rolls over Bernal.
Start with fog, end with fog, and in between: the bison in Golden Gate Park, paddle boats, and hot dogs that taste better because we walked six miles.
Church in the Mission, then twenty of us taking over one corner of Dolores Park like we hold a permit. Someone always brings a guitar.
East Bay cousins in on BART by ten, Chinatown for buns, then the cable car ride we swear we'll never do again. We do it every single year.
Clement Street groceries in three languages, mahjong at the apartment all afternoon, dinner assembled from four different takeout bags.
Fort Funston with the dogs at nine, a sandy car forever after, burritos eaten in total silence because they are too good to talk over.
Roughly: fog, pancakes, one argument about parking versus Muni, Muni winning, Golden Gate Park until the kids collapse, early dinner in the Richmond.
An Ocean Beach bonfire at dusk, everyone wearing every jacket we own, the whole day built backwards from that single hour.
The wave organ at high tide with grandpa, who calls it the sea singing. Then chowder somewhere touristy, because he likes watching the boats.
No plan, one rule: we end the day on the bench above the Sunset when the fog pours in. Fifteen years of that same bench.

33.text: Buy the house on the corner. Yes, that one, the ugly one. Empty the savings account. You will thank me from the porch.
The store will fail, and it will turn out to be the best thing that ever happens to us. Don't waste two years being ashamed of it.
Record grandma's stories now. All of them, even the ones she insists nobody wants to hear. Especially those ones.
Go to the airport together, all of you, for every arrival and every departure. You will not always be able to.
The fights about the restaurant were never about the restaurant. Say the real thing sooner. It saves you about six years.
Please write the WiFi password down somewhere. Also, be nicer to the middle kid. She turns out to be right about nearly everything.
Learn her dumpling folds now, with your hands, not your phone. The video you keep meaning to take does not exist.
He isn't lazy, he's drowning. Ask the question twice. In this family it is always the second ask that works.
Take the trip to the village while all four grandparents can still manage the walk up from the bus stop.
You survive all of it. The diagnosis, the layoff, the flooded kitchen. You even laugh about the kitchen. Start laughing sooner.
To the grown-ups: back up the photos twice. To everyone: the group chat you will eventually start becomes the family's living room. Start it now.
The quiet kid in the corner is listening to everything. Watch what you say about her weight and her chances.
Hug him at the door every single time, even when you are furious about the motorcycle. You will want those hugs back.
Your English is enough. Take the class, sit the license exam, ask for the raise. Fifteen years is a long time to whisper.
Keep the ugly green couch. I am completely serious. Every good decision this family ever makes gets made on that couch.
You are not behind. Every family at every dinner table is improvising. Loosen your grip a little and enjoy the noise.

35.text: The turkey slid off the platter, across the floor, and under the table. Grandma declared 'five second rule' in front of God and everybody. We ate it.
We drove four hours to the reunion a full week early. Stood in an empty park holding forty deviled eggs. Ate them in the car. No regrets.
The karaoke machine would not turn off, so every speech at the anniversary had backing music. My uncle's toast, in autotune. Cinema.
Mom washed my brother's passport the morning of the flight. We now know every employee at that consulate. We exchange holiday cards.
Two aunts secretly swapped sugar for salt to sabotage the same bake-off and cancelled each other out. The cake was fine. The truth took years.
The tent collapsed at two in the morning and we all just lay there underneath it like a quesadilla, laughing too hard to fix anything.
Dad proudly grilled the decorative wax fruit, convinced it was real. The smell lasted a season. The nickname lasted much longer.
Locked out during the toddler's nap, so my seventy-year-old mother went through the window like a professional. The neighbors applauded.
The wedding cake melted in the trunk, so we served it in bowls with spoons and called it trifle. Guests still request 'the trifle.'
Grandpa wandered into the wrong funeral for twenty minutes and made friends. We had to physically retrieve him. He still sends that family cards.
Everyone brought potato salad to the picnic. Seven bowls. No plates, no forks, no other food. We ate potato salad with chips, like heroes.
The quinceañera dove refused to leave its box. Just stared at us. My uncle made eye contact with it, said 'same,' and the whole church lost it.
The GPS delivered us to a cornfield instead of the hotel, and my father, on principle, refused to admit it for forty-five minutes of corn.
We flushed the goldfish with full honors, then found the actual goldfish behind the filter, alive. Explaining the resurrection to a five-year-old was theological work.
The smoke alarm went off during grace six Thanksgivings running. It is part of grace now. We pause for it, heads still bowed.
Someone microwaved the frozen jar of starter my grandmother carried from the old country. The bang. The silence. Her face. We laugh now, quietly.

37.text: My parents at nineteen, on the boat over, before any of us existed. I want to see their faces from before the worry set in.
All four generations in one frame. We overlapped for exactly eleven days, and nobody thought to find a camera that week.
My grandmother laughing so hard at my grandfather that she slid off the kitchen chair. I can hear it perfectly. I just can't show anyone.
The kitchen of the first apartment, mid-dinner. Bad light, steam, elbows everywhere, the whole family caught mid-sentence.
Dad asleep in the recliner with the baby asleep on his chest, both mouths open. We saw it a hundred times and photographed it never.
My mother during the night shift years, in her uniform, before we understood what she was carrying. I would frame it in gold.
The blackout dinner. Candles, cold noodles, shadow puppets on the wall. No proof it happened, but every one of us remembers it.
Grandpa teaching my mother to ride a bike in the temple courtyard, and her teaching me in a parking lot. Same photo, forty years apart, hung side by side.
The exact second the fish spat the hook and my uncle went in after it. The retelling has been contested for thirty years. One photo would end wars.
All of us on the roof watching fireworks the summer before the move. Somebody said 'remember this' and nobody raised a phone. Good. And also, I wish.
My grandmother as a girl, before the war took the albums. She describes one photo from memory: braids, a bicycle, a gate. I'd give a lot for that gate.
The five of us crammed into the old hatchback with a mattress on the roof. Moving day. Everyone furious, everyone young.
My parents' first dance at their wedding. The photographer's film was ruined. Forty years later they will re-enact it in the kitchen if you ask nicely.
Me and my great-grandmother, who died two months before I was born. Everyone says we would have gotten along scary well. One photo. That's all I want.
Sunday mornings, all the shoes piled at the door of the old flat, tiny up to enormous. Nobody photographs shoes. Somebody should have.
The moment my father opened the citizenship letter and did the one dance he knows. The dance survives. The letter is framed. The moment isn't.

39.text: The smell of rice hitting a hot pan in my neighbor's apartment at six o'clock. Suddenly I was ten years old and setting the table.
Someone on the bus peeled an orange in one long unbroken spiral, the way grandpa insists is the only way. I almost said something.
I found a rubber band on my doorknob and realized I had put it there myself. The drawer lives on in me. There is no escaping the drawer.
A stranger's grandmother at the pharmacy told me to wear a scarf. I wore the scarf. Every one of you would have approved.
My roommate double-checked the stove before we left, and I heard mom's voice say 'better safe.' So I checked it a third time.
Wednesday's fog rolled in over the avenues at exactly four, right on our old walk-to-dinner schedule. I took the walk anyway, alone.
I caught myself narrating the GPS's mistakes out loud, alone in the car, in my father's exact wounded tone of voice.
The market had the first good persimmons of the year. I bought eight before remembering I am one person now. Four are going in the mail.
A kid at the laundromat was losing a card game to his grandmother, who was very clearly cheating. Dynasty behavior. Ours exactly.
I was humming over midnight noodles and realized halfway through that it was her dish-washing song. It got quiet in my kitchen after that.
Somebody double-parked outside the bakery with the flashers on, obviously grabbing the family's usual Saturday order. Respect. Deep respect.
My phone surfaced an old beach day. Everyone squinting, nobody ready, sand in the sandwiches. Perfect. Straight to the group chat.
I wrote 'some' as a measurement while sharing a recipe and had to explain this entire family to one very confused coworker.
I rinsed out the salsa jar and kept it. For nothing in particular. For everything, really. A good jar is a good jar.
The 1 California went by with a kid asleep on his mother's shoulder, backpack still on, and there we all were, every version of us.
It rained during my run and instead of taking shelter I got loud and happy about it, which I understand now is an inherited condition.
